client: Honestly, I've been feeling really overwhelmed with school lately. Ever since I got that C in calculus last semester, I can't stop worrying about my GPA and how it might ruin my chances for grad school. I know one bad grade isn't the end of the world, but I keep beating myself up about it and now I'm terrified of slipping up again this semester.
therapist: It sounds like this situation with your grades has left you feeling quite anxious and self-critical. The way you're catastrophizing about one grade affecting your entire future suggests your thoughts might be running away with worst-case scenarios. What evidence do you have that supports or challenges these fears about grad school?

client: I know logically that one grade doesn’t define everything, but it’s hard to shake the feeling that I’ve already ruined my chances. I keep thinking about how competitive grad school admissions are, and I worry that this one slip-up will make me stand out in a bad way. It’s like my mind keeps looping back to the worst possible outcome no matter how much I try to reason with it.
therapist: I hear how stuck you feel in this cycle of negative thinking, even though part of you knows the reality might be different. The way your mind keeps returning to these worst-case scenarios suggests this grade has become a sort of mental "sticky point" for you. What would it feel like to imagine a scenario where this grade actually didn't impact your future as much as you fear?

client: I get what you're saying, but it's hard to imagine that scenario because this grade feels so important right now. My mind keeps going to how it'll look on my transcript and how it might ruin my chances for grad school. Even if I try to picture it not mattering, it just feels unrealistic because the competition is so intense.
therapist: I can see how real and immediate this worry feels for you right now, even though the intensity of your reaction suggests this thought might be carrying more weight than it objectively deserves. When you say it feels unrealistic to imagine it not mattering, that makes me wonder - what would need to happen for you to start seeing this situation with a bit more perspective?

client: I don't know what would make me see it differently - that's the problem. The worry just feels so true and important in the moment, even though part of me knows I'm probably overreacting. It's like my brain keeps coming back to "but what if this time is different?" no matter how I try to reason with myself.
therapist: The way you describe this mental tug-of-war—where part of you recognizes the overreaction while another part insists "but what if?"—sounds exhausting. That persistent "what if" voice seems to have a strong grip right now. Rather than trying to argue with it directly, what if we approached this anxious part with curiosity? What do you think it's trying to protect you from by keeping you so focused on this grade?

client: I think that anxious voice is trying to protect me from failing and disappointing my parents again. But it's so loud all the time now that I can't even focus on studying, which just makes me more anxious. Part of me knows this isn't helpful, but another part thinks if I don't worry constantly, I'll slack off and fail for real.
therapist: It sounds like this anxiety has become a double-edged sword - trying to motivate you but actually making it harder to function. That inner conflict between knowing the worry isn't helpful yet fearing what might happen if you let go of it must feel paralyzing. What do you think might happen if you experimented with setting aside just 10% of that worry energy and redirecting it toward focused study time?

client:
I get what you're saying, but the anxiety feels like my safety net. If I try to let go even a little, I'm scared I'll completely lose control and fall behind. It's like my brain thinks the constant worrying is the only thing keeping me from failing. 

Also, when I'm anxious, I can't even focus enough to study properly - my mind just races in circles about everything I need to do. How am I supposed to redirect that energy when it feels so overwhelming?
therapist: I hear how trapped you feel between needing the anxiety to stay "safe" and recognizing it's actually making things harder. That racing, overwhelmed feeling when you try to study suggests your brain is stuck in threat mode. What if we tried breaking this cycle by starting with just one small, manageable study task—something so simple the anxious part might relax its grip a little?

client: I get what you're saying about starting small, but even that feels overwhelming right now. My brain keeps screaming that if I don't study everything perfectly, I'll fail and ruin my future. And when I've tried small tasks before, I still end up spiraling about all the other things I'm not getting done.
therapist: It sounds like that perfectionist voice has taken over completely, making even small steps feel impossible right now. The way you describe your brain "screaming" suggests this anxiety has become all-consuming. What would it be like to notice that voice without believing it - to observe it like an overprotective but misguided friend?

client: That sounds nice in theory, but when my brain starts screaming at me about all the ways I'm failing, it's not just some quiet little voice I can observe. It feels like my whole body tenses up and I can't think straight. Like last night when I stayed up until 3am rewriting a simple work email fifteen times because it never felt good enough.
therapist: I hear how physically intense this experience is for you - the tension, the late nights, the compulsive rewriting. This isn't just mental worry; it's taken over your body and behaviors in a very real way. When you're in that moment of rewriting for the fifteenth time, what's the smallest interruption you could imagine inserting to disrupt that cycle? Even just standing up to stretch for 30 seconds?

client: I know I should try to interrupt the cycle, but when I'm in that rewriting frenzy, even standing up feels impossible. My brain screams that if I stop for even a second, I'll miss some critical mistake that'll ruin everything. The idea of pausing makes my chest tighten even more.
therapist: I can see how completely this perfectionism has you in its grip—where even a brief pause feels physically impossible because the stakes feel so catastrophically high. That chest-tightening response shows how deeply your body has learned to react to these thoughts. What if we approached this very gently: instead of trying to stop the rewriting, could you simply notice and name what's happening in those moments? Like saying to yourself "Ah, there's that perfectionist urge again"?

client: I get what you're saying about noticing the urge, but I don't see how that actually helps. When I'm in that panicked rewriting mode, just labeling it feels too passive—like I'm still failing to fix whatever's wrong with my work. The tightness in my chest gets worse when I try to just observe instead of act.
therapist: I hear how frustrating it feels when well-meaning suggestions seem too passive—like they're ignoring the real urgency you're experiencing. That tightness in your chest shows how physically demanding this perfectionism has become. What if we reframed "noticing" not as doing nothing, but as practicing a different kind of action—one that creates space between you and those intense urges? How might that feel different from just passively observing?
